title: Short-Lived LLMs, Long-Lived Decisions: the UAE and the Challenge of Keeping Government AI Reliable as Findings Expire
content: The shelf life of LLM findings and the lifespan of large language model (LLM) families in science are currently shrinking. At the same time, governments increasingly use LLMs to support decisions whose consequences may persist for years, even as the used models vanish and findings about them lose validity. A reassessment of published LLM claims classified 44% as expired and 34% as weakened on newer models. Separate research suggests shorter scientific adoption lifecycles for more recently released models. A recent OECD survey documents extensive governmental AI adoption, while post-deployment audits are less common. In more than 90% of OECD countries, the scientific evidence behind government AI decisions may be outdated long before the decisions are implemented. This narrative review examines what is required to maintain reliable government AI under these conditions. It brings together studies of LLM findings’ persistence, model adoption, politically consequential behavior, and evaluation methods with OECD governance evidence and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) case. The UAE ranks first in Microsoft's latest AI Diffusion reports on generative AI use. Given its level of adoption and the pace of its government plans, the UAE may be among the first, if not the first, to face the shelf life problem. The UAE combines domestic model development, shared government services, sovereign hosting, and collaborations with frontier model developers, backed by more than USD 30 billion in announced national and international investment. Even so, keeping government AI reliable requires maintenance effort that remains likely underestimated. We propose five recommendations for governments.
